conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes I’d like to use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (the EPDS) to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply a 10-question screen that helps us spot common mood changes—nothing you say will leave this room unless safety requires it, and there are no right or wrong answers. We’ll go question by question; just share what feels true for you. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, looking back, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
Um… I guess I can still laugh, but it doesn’t come as easily. Like, my partner will make a joke and I’ll smile, but it feels kind of forced. I don’t get that light, happy feeling I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I wouldn’t say that. I mean, I’ve laughed a couple of times, but it’s not the same—more like I’m going through the motions rather than really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but lately even those feel like chores. I still go, and once I’m there it’s… okay, but the looking-forward part barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. Like, if the baby wouldn’t settle, I’d catch myself thinking I must be doing something wrong or that I’m not a good enough mom. I know it’s probably not true, but the thought still pops in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little. Sometimes I’ll suddenly worry that the baby isn’t breathing right or that I missed something important at her last check-up, even when everything looks fine. It doesn’t last long—I can talk myself down—but it still comes out of nowhere and makes my chest tight for a minute.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky, no. I get those quick flashes of “what if something bad happens?” but they pass before I feel truly scared. I haven’t had any full-blown panic or heart-racing moments.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah. Most days I keep everything moving—feedings, diapers, laundry—but every so often it feels like the next thing on the list might tip me over. Yesterday I almost cried because I couldn’t find the clean burp cloths, even though I knew it wasn’t a big deal. I pull myself together pretty quickly, but those moments catch me off guard.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, it’s not that bad. I do get to sleep; it just takes me a little longer some nights when my mind keeps running through the day. Once I’m out, I’m out—only the baby’s crying wakes me.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes, a bit. I’d say I feel sad or kind of flat a few days each week. It’s not there all the time—sometimes I’ll be holding the baby and feel okay—but then it creeps back in like a little gray cloud. Nothing crushing, just… blah.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried a couple of times this week. Once was when the baby wouldn’t nap and I felt like I was failing, and another time I just got overwhelmed looking at the mess in the kitchen. It wasn’t all-day sobbing or anything—just tears for a few minutes, then I wiped my face and kept going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I get frustrated or down, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind. I just want to feel like myself again.

You've shared that while you're managing daily tasks, laughter feels forced and things you once anticipated now feel like chores. You notice self-blame when the baby won't settle, fleeting worries about her safety, and a flat or sad mood that drifts in several days a week. Moments of overwhelm bring tears, yet you summon energy to keep going. You're not having thoughts of harming yourself; you simply want to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to genuinely enjoy humor, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports a clear reduction in anticipatory enjoyment—plans feel like chores and the sense of looking forward is barely present—aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a few times this week" which aligns with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes specific, recurring intrusive worries about the baby's health that arise without cause and cause physical anxiety symptoms, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and near-tears over a minor incident, indicating intermittent difficulty coping.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, quite often"—sadness is present several days per week.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 14 meets the EPDS cutoff for probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Key indicators include persistent low mood (<sym>sadness</sym> several days/week), marked loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), self-reproach about parenting competence, episodes of crying triggered by minor stressors, and anxious intrusive thoughts about infant safety. Item 10 is negative, indicating no current self-harm ideation. Per DSM-5 criteria, five or more depressive symptoms present most days for two weeks warrant clinical evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full assessment
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>CBT</med> or, if indicated, <med>sertraline</med>
3. Schedule EPDS re-screen in two weeks to monitor trend
4. Encourage 15-20 min daily outdoor walks and balanced meals to support mood
5. Plan partner/family member to handle one night feeding so you can obtain 4-5 hrs uninterrupted sleep
6. Provide crisis hotline numbers: Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773, National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 1-833-943-5746
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [enter date] – 6–8 wks post-delivery, self-report on EPDS-10 items

Symptoms / Observations  
• Persistent low mood (Q8) several days/wk; anhedonia (Q1, Q2)  
• Excessive self-blame / guilt re parenting competence (Q3)  
• Episodic tearfulness triggered by minor stressors (Q9)  
• Transient, intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety; mild autonomic arousal (tight chest) without frank panic (Q4, Q5)  
• Subjective overwhelm and near-tearfulness when routine tasks accumulate (Q6)  
• Mild initial insomnia related to mental rumination; no middle/late insomnia (Q7)  
• Denies self-harm ideation (Q10)

Pattern Summary  
Mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms (sadness, loss of pleasure, guilt) with comorbid situational anxiety; functional tasks maintained but with emotional effort and distress.

Screening Significance  
Score range: approximately 9–11 (if formally tallied) – above typical 7-cutoff for further evaluation; meets threshold for possible minor/major depressive episode with anxious features in postpartum context.

Risk Factors Present  
– Recurrent crying, low enjoyment, self-criticism  
– Anxiety spikes regarding infant well-being  
– No safety concerns voiced (negative self-harm item)

Recommendation for Follow-up  
Refer for structured clinical interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS re-score) and consideration of brief evidence-based intervention; monitor safety at every contact.
